correctness.rationale: After appending b the entire set of distinct subsequences ending in b is exactly {wb: w is an old subsequence, possibly empty}: old words ending in b are included in this image, not counted a second time. Words ending in the other symbol are unchanged. Thus the two shifted coordinates start at (1,1), add one to the other, and sum to H_n, not C_n. The expectation matrix has eigenvalues 1±sqrt(t) and output values 2,3 at n=0,1, giving the mean. Expanding the three quadratic monomials gives the stated positive matrix T_p. In λ−1 coordinates its characteristic polynomial is (λ−1)^3−5t(λ−1)−2t. Cayley–Hamilton gives the moment recurrence, whose first values are 4,9,16+18t (the n=2 outcomes are H=4 or 5); multiplying the OGF by its denominator gives numerator 4−3z+(1−2t)z². At λ=(1+s)^2 the characteristic polynomial is s²(s⁴+6s³+7s²−2s−2); the parenthesis is strictly convex on [0,1/2] with endpoint values −2 and −7/16, hence is negative. This gives a larger real root; for interior p strict positivity gives a simple dominant Perron root and a positive scalar projection onto it. It exceeds the squared-mean exponential rate, so subtracting the squared mean leaves the leading second-moment growth. In the fair case symmetry eliminates the antisymmetric eigenmode at 1/2 and the remaining two eigenvalues have sum 5/2 and product 1/2; initial M_0,M_1 give the stated coefficients. The endpoints p=0,1 are deterministic C_n=n+1. The growth is asymptotic for fixed interior p, not a finite-n strict monotonicity statement, not uniform near the endpoints, and not a result about convergence in probability. Independent replay `python3 /workspace/reproduce_reviews.py 1` explicitly enumerated index-subset outputs through length 9 and matched 70 exact bias/length cases, including deterministic endpoints and the fair quadratic recurrence. The frozen verifier was read, not executed.

The strict rate separation throughout the nondegenerate bias range gives a quantitative obstruction to relative L² concentration, not a single numerical instance or a claim about typical deviations unsupported by moments. The rational law can also be used to evaluate finite biased variances exactly.
